summaries.example: Imagine sorting a classroom’s objects into labeled boxes: numbers go in one box, truth answers in another, and rules that take numbers as inputs go in a third. A type is like a label that tells us what kind of thing an expression is. A function can be used one step at a time. For example, a two-step adding rule can first take 3 and then take 4, giving 7. The lambda symbol lets us describe such a rule: “the rule that takes a number n and gives 4n+3.” Applying it to 5 gives 23.
summaries.summary: Church’s type theory, also called simple type theory, is a carefully designed language for logic. It gives every expression a type, or kind. Numbers, truth values, sets, and functions are treated as different kinds of things. A function may take one input and return another function, which lets the language describe rules with several inputs. The lambda symbol describes a function by telling us what it does to an input. A set or property can also be represented by a function that returns true for members and false for nonmembers. Because the types must fit together, an expression that would create Russell’s paradox is not allowed. The system includes familiar logic, such as “not,” “or,” and “for every,” and it can be used to describe mathematics, plans, and computer programs. More advanced versions help computers check proofs and reason about formal statements.
key_ideas: Church’s type theory is a formal language for expressing logical and mathematical ideas.
Every expression has a type, which helps keep different kinds of things from being mixed up.
Sets, properties, and relations can be represented as special kinds of functions.
The lambda symbol describes functions, and applying a function can replace its input with a chosen value.
Careful types help avoid the kind of contradiction found in Russell’s paradox.
The theory can support proof assistants, software checking, mathematics, and some language and artificial-intelligence research.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory gives people and computers a precise way to describe complicated ideas. Its type labels can block certain confusing combinations before they cause trouble. This makes it useful for writing mathematics, checking whether software and hardware meet specifications, and building systems that search for proofs. It also shows how a small collection of formal rules can express many different kinds of knowledge.

important_terms.definition: A label showing what kind of thing an expression stands for, such as a number, truth value, set, or function.
A rule that takes an input of one type and gives an output of another type.
A way to describe a function by showing what it does to an input; Church’s theory uses the symbol λ.
An expression that follows the rules of the formal language and has a permitted type.

summaries.example: Let σ be the type of natural numbers. A function that takes a natural number and returns a natural number has type (σσ), using Church’s notation. The addition function can be treated as a one-input function whose output is another one-input function: after receiving x, it returns the function that adds x to y. Lambda notation represents the rule that sends n to 4n+3 as λn(4n+3). Applying it to 5 reduces to 4·5+3, or 23. The same framework can represent a property as a function from objects to truth values and a relation as a function that takes two objects and returns truth or falsehood.

Church’s type theory, also called simple type theory, is a formal language that extends propositional and first-order logic with higher-order resources. Its basic discipline is typing: every entity belongs to a type, and a function type records both the input and output types. If α and β are types, Church writes (αβ) for functions from β-objects to α-objects. Functions with several arguments can be represented as chains of one-argument functions, a technique illustrated by curried addition. Properties and sets can be represented by characteristic functions into the type o of truth values, while relations are functions returning truth values after several applications.

The formal expressions are called well-formed formulas in the entry’s terminology, although only those of type o are assertions in the more usual terminology. Lambda abstraction forms functions: λx A denotes the function whose value at an argument is obtained by substituting that argument for the free occurrences of x in A. Beta-conversion describes this application and has important normalization and uniqueness results. Quantification can be defined using a property that holds of the set of all objects of a type, so lambda abstraction supplies the needed binding mechanism. Equality may be defined in a Leibnizian way through shared properties, or taken as primitive in the alternative formulation Q0.

key_ideas: Church’s formulation is a higher-order logical language: it permits quantification over individuals and also over functions, properties, and relations.
Types distinguish individuals, truth values, sets, and functions of increasingly complex kinds. This blocks ill-formed self-membership constructions associated with Russell’s paradox.

Functions are primitive in the framework. Relations and properties can be treated as functions into truth values, and several-argument functions can be represented through successive one-argument applications.
Lambda abstraction is the only variable-binding mechanism required in the basic presentation; quantifiers and description expressions can be defined or introduced using it.

Church’s theory has elementary logic and can be extended with extensionality, descriptions, choice, and infinity principles. Some formulations instead take equality as primitive and define other logical operators from it.

The source distinguishes standard models, which contain all functions of the relevant types, from general or Henkin models, which contain selected function collections. The completeness theorem concerns general semantics, while validity in standard models is stronger and is not captured by the same recursively axiomatized system.
summaries.why_it_matters: Church’s type theory combines expressive power with strict formal control. It can represent mathematical structures, software and hardware specifications, natural-language meanings, and other logical systems embedded inside it. Proof assistants and automated theorem provers use related systems to check formal mathematics and programs. The same expressiveness creates technical costs: higher-order unification is undecidable in general, proof search is more difficult than in first-order logic, and the distinction between standard and general semantics affects what completeness means. Studying the theory therefore connects philosophical questions about formal representation with practical workพૅ

important_terms.definition: A formal category assigned to every entity. If α and β are types, (αβ) is the type of functions from β to α.
An expression of the formal language that has a permitted structure and type. In Church’s terminology, expressions of many types can be wffs; only type o expressions function as assertions.
The operator λ that constructs a function from an expression containing a variable, such as λx A.
The process of replacing an application of a lambda-defined function by the result of putting its argument into the function’s body.
A function from objects to truth values that represents membership in a set or possession of a property.
The principle that functions with identical values for every argument are identical; Church’s theory includes functional extensionality among its additional principles.
A semantics in which each function type may contain a selected collection of functions rather than every possible function. Henkin’s completeness result applies to this general notion of model.
A formal operator used for “the object satisfying” a condition, or, with the axiom of choice, for selecting an object satisfying it when one exists.

summaries.example: Suppose a school is planning a trip with several stops. A “plan” can be represented as a function: give it a time, and it returns the state of the trip at that time. A state records where the people and animals are. We can then define an acceptable plan as one that starts at the hotel, ends at the farm, and never leaves the ostrich and cheetah together without their owner. The statement “there is an acceptable plan” can be written using an existential quantifier over plans. The types matter: times, places, states, and plans are different sorts of things, so the formal language helps prevent us from applying the wrong rule to the wrong object.
summaries.summary:
Church’s type theory, or simple type theory, is a formal logical language designed to express more than ordinary propositional and first-order logic. Its central rule is that every entity has a type. Types may stand for individuals, truth values, or functions between types. A function with several arguments is represented by applying one argument at a time: after the first input, the result can be another function waiting for the next input. This makes the language compact while preserving a clear account of inputs and outputs.

The theory treats functions as basic. A property can be represented by a function from objects to truth values, and a relation can be represented by a function that eventually returns a truth value. A lambda expression describes a function directly. For instance, λn(4n+3) represents the function that sends a natural number n to 4n+3. When this function is applied to 5, beta-conversion replaces n with 5 and produces 23. Quantifiers can be expressed using lambda abstraction and special constants that describe properties of all objects of a type.

Church’s system includes rules for logic and lambda-conversion. It can also be extended with principles such as Boolean and functional extensionality, description operators, the axiom of choice, and axioms of infinity. One formulation defines equality using the idea that identical objects share properties; another formulation, Q0, takes equality as primitive and defines several other logical notions from it. The source also explains two kinds of semantics. Standard models include every function between the relevant domains, while Henkin or general models may include only selected function collections. key_ideas: Church’s type theory is a higher-order logic: it can quantify over individuals as well as properties, relations, and functions.
Types organize the language and stop expressions from mixing incompatible kinds of objects.
A property can be represented as a function that returns a truth value, and a set can be treated similarly.
Lambda abstraction describes functions. Applying a lambda expression works by substituting an input into its body, a process called beta-conversion.
The system has different possible additions, including extensionality, descriptions, choice, and infinity. These are not all the same as the basic logical core.
There is a difference between standard models, containing all functions of the relevant types, and Henkin models, containing selected collections. This difference matters for completeness.
summaries.why_it_matters: This theory matters because it provides one formal language for describing mathematics, programs, hardware, natural-language meanings, and other logical systems. Its strict type discipline helps avoid contradictions that arise when arbitrary sets or expressions are allowed to refer to themselves in unrestricted ways. Its expressive power also supports proof assistants and automated theorem provers. At the same time, higher-order reasoning is difficult: some unification problems are undecidable, and the larger language creates a much bigger proof-search space than first-order logic. Thus the theory illustrates both the benefits and costs of making a formal language more expressive.

important_terms.definition: A formal label for a kind of object. It tells the system whether an expression is an individual, truth value, function, or something more complex.
A rule that takes an object of one type and returns an object of another type. A multi-step function can be represented as a chain of one-step functions.
A symbol, λ, used to build a function by describing what happens to an input.
A permitted expression in the language. Its symbols fit together according to the grammar and its type requirements.
A way to express “for every” or “there exists” by ranging over objects of a specified type.
The claim that two functions are the same when they give the same output for every permitted input.
An interpretation with selected collections of functions at each type. It is broader than a standard model and supports the relevant completeness theorem.
A rule saying that a choice can be made from every nonempty set, when that principle is included in the theory.
